Contrast enhanced CT abdomen revealed the presence of a MD with thickened, enhancing walls associated with inflammatory changes in the adjacent fat (Figure 4). The normal appendix was identified separately on CT, resulting in a diagnosis of Meckel’s diverticulitis. The patient underwent laparoscopically assisted trans-umbilical Meckel’s diverticulectomy. Histopathology confirmed the imaging diagnosis.

panels.figure_caption: Microscopy image H&E staining of Meckel's diverticulum. A) (10x), B) (40x) It reveals the presence of glandular structures that consist of cuboidal cells, which collectively form the pancreatic acini (PA) exhibiting intense hematoxylin staining. In addition, the image reveals the existence of islets of Langerhans (IL), comprising polygonal cells with voluminous and pale cytoplasm and monomorphic nuclei with classic salt and pepper chromatin. Furthermore, the pancreatic ducts are visible, lined with low cuboidal epithelium that has uniform nuclei alternating with the pancreatic acini. The tissue in question is classified as an ectopic pancreatic tissue type 1 as per the Heinrich classification, owing to the presence of centroacinous cells (CC), excretory ducts (ED), and IL.
in_text_mentions: During the histopathological examination, an MD measuring 3.5 cm x 2 cm with a whitish-yellow invaginated area was observed macroscopically. The hematoxylin and eosin staining analysis of the histological section revealed a Meckel's diverticulum with Heinrich type 1 ectopic pancreatic tissue implantation, and no signs of malignancy were found (Figure 3).

EP are classified using the Heinrich criteria, which distinguish three types. Type 1 is characterized by the presence of acini, excretory ducts, and islets of Langerhans (IL). Type 2 presents acini and excretory ducts, while type 3 only contains excretory ducts. The most prevalent type is type 2, followed by type 1, while type 3 is the least commonly encountered [8]. In our case, the histopathological classification of the PE corresponded to Heinrich type 1, which is less frequent, with only a few reported cases (Figure 3).

source_variant.figure_caption: Microscopy image H&E staining of Meckel's diverticulum. A) (10x), B) (40x) It reveals the presence of glandular structures that consist of cuboidal cells, which collectively form the pancreatic acini (PA) exhibiting intense hematoxylin staining. In addition, the image reveals the existence of islets of Langerhans (IL), comprising polygonal cells with voluminous and pale cytoplasm and monomorphic nuclei with classic salt and pepper chromatin. Furthermore, the pancreatic ducts are visible, lined with low cuboidal epithelium that has uniform nuclei alternating with the pancreatic acini. The tissue in question is classified as an ectopic pancreatic tissue type 1 as per the Heinrich classification, owing to the presence of centroacinous cells (CC), excretory ducts (ED), and IL.

Referencing risk factors for asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum [4], elective surgical resection was proposed for secondary prevention of complications. The patient consented to laparoscopic Meckel's diverticulum resection. The Meckel's diverticulum resection margins were set approximately 30 mm from the pseudodiverticulum, allowing for complete excision of the Meckel's diverticulum. The resected specimen confirmed the presence of a diverticulum within the Meckel's diverticulum (Figure 2), without evidence of perforation in the Meckel's diverticulum itself.

A: Gross pathology photograph clearly shows a giant Meckel's diverticulum attached to small intestine, with dusky/necrotic appearance; black arrow marks the lesion. B: H&E microscopic panel from the Meckel diverticulum specimen shows transmural necrosis and vascular congestion; no ectopic tissue is present and no configured vocabulary finding directly matches. C: H&E microscopic panel from the Meckel diverticulum specimen shows transmural necrosis and mural congestion; findings are pathological complications of the Meckel diverticulum but are not represented in the configured vocabulary. D: High-power H&E image shows acute inflammatory infiltrate in the serosa of the Meckel's diverticulum, supporting complicated Meckel diverticulum; no configured vocabulary finding directly matches histologic serosal inflammation.
